title: Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets
statement: A garden is a row of flowers, and flower `i` opens on day `bloomDay[i]`, so on day `d` every flower with `bloomDay[i] <= d` is open. A bouquet takes exactly `k` open flowers that stand next to each other in the row, and no flower may be used in more than one bouquet. Return the earliest day on which `m` bouquets can be made, or `-1` if the garden can never supply `m` bouquets.
signature: int minDays(int[] bloomDay, int m, int k)
notes:
## Intuition

Waiting longer never hurts: every flower open on day `d` is still open on day `d + 1`, so "can we make `m` bouquets by day `d`?" is false up to some day and true from then on. That monotone yes/no lets us binary search on the day instead of trying every candidate day (the brute force tries each distinct bloom day in order and counts bouquets each time, O(n²)).

## Approach

1. If `m * k` exceeds the number of flowers, no day is enough: return `-1`.
2. Otherwise the answer lies in `[low, high] = [1, max(bloomDay)]`, because by the last bloom day every flower is open.
3. While `low < high`, test `mid`: scan the row, growing `streak` for each flower open by `mid` and resetting it at a closed one; whenever `streak` reaches `k`, count a bouquet and start a new streak.
4. If `bouquets >= m`, `mid` works, so keep it: `high = mid`. Otherwise the answer is later: `low = mid + 1`.
5. When the range shrinks to one day, return `low`.

## Example 1, step by step

`bloomDay = [1, 10, 3, 10, 2]`, `m = 3`, `k = 1`. `m * k = 3 <= 5`, so search `[1, 10]`.

- `mid = 5`: open flowers are days 1, 3, 2, giving 3 bouquets, so `high = 5`.
- `mid = 3`: again 3 bouquets, `high = 3`.
- `mid = 2`: only days 1 and 2, 2 bouquets, `low = 3`.

`low = high = 3`, the answer.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log D), where D is the largest bloom day: about 30 halvings, each a linear scan.
- Space: O(1) extra.

## Pitfalls

- Check `m * k > n` first; without it the search returns `max(bloomDay)` even when the bouquets are impossible. In languages with 32-bit ints, `m * k` can overflow (up to 10^11), so use a 64-bit product.
- Reset `streak` both at a closed flower and after completing a bouquet, so no flower is used twice.
- Use `high = mid` (not `mid - 1`) when `mid` works, or the true answer can be skipped.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `low`, `high` | the range of days that may still be the answer |
| `mid` | the day being tested |
| `bouquets` | bouquets that can be made by day `mid` |
| `streak` | open adjacent flowers not yet used in a bouquet |
| `day` | bloom day of the flower being scanned |

narration.2: If there are fewer flowers than m * k, no amount of waiting is enough.
narration.3: Report the impossible case right away.
narration.5: Day 1 is the earliest possible answer.
narration.6: By the latest bloom day every flower is open, so that day always works here.
narration.8: Narrow the range until a single day remains.
narration.9: Test the day in the middle of the range.
narration.12: Walk along the row of flowers.
narration.13: This flower is open by day mid.
narration.14: It extends the current run of adjacent open flowers.
narration.15: The run has exactly k flowers, enough for one bouquet.
narration.17: ...and start a fresh run so these flowers are not reused.
narration.20: A closed flower breaks the run.
narration.23: Enough bouquets by day mid: the answer is mid or earlier.
narration.26: Too few bouquets: the answer is after mid.
narration.29: The range has shrunk to the earliest day that works.
